title: If 1 trading bot survives out of 50 variants, when does it stop being “luck”?
author: GreatBreadfruit8139
selftext:
I’ve been thinking about this after building a public Paper-trading League for crypto bots and getting some good criticism from other traders.

Suppose you create 50 different variants of the same strategy.

Different exits. Different RSI thresholds. Different DCA settings. Different timeframes. Different combinations of filters.

In the League, every bot is frozen from the moment it is created.

So you are not continually tweaking one bot until the chart looks good. You are creating 50 separate fixed experiments, each with its own configuration and its own forward record.

Naturally, one of them may start outperforming the others.

At that point, the obvious criticism is:

“You tested 50 variants. Of course one of them looks good by chance.”

And I think that criticism is fair at the beginning.

But this is the part I find interesting:

What happens if that exact same frozen bot just keeps running?

No changes to the configuration.

many trades and many months.. Different volatility regimes.. A major BTC drawdown.. Maybe a long sideways period... And it still keeps performing while controlling drawdown.

At what point does the fact that it originally came from 50 variants become less important than the new evidence it has accumulated afterward?

My view is:

I wouls care less about how a strategy was discovered, and more about whether it keeps surviving after discovery.

The large search space should absolutely remain visible as context.

But I don’t think a bot should be permanently dismissed just because it came from a large family of experiments.

If it keeps surviving unchanged, the market is continuously adding new evidence.

That makes me think the useful thing is not to hide the family history, but to show it clearly.

For example, a public bot record could show:

* number of sibling variants
* date the bot was first created
* number of trades since creation
* number of trades since it started standing out from the family
* return
* profit factor
* max drawdown
* market exposure
* BTC and ETH return over the exact same period
* major market drawdowns survived
* whether the configuration ever changed
* all retired or failed siblings

That last point matters to me too.

If 49 variants failed and 1 survived, I don’t want the 49 failures to disappear.

I’d rather show the whole family and let people judge the survivor in context.

This is basically the direction I’m taking with the public Bot League I’m building inside LabNarrative.

Each crypto Spot bot runs as its own Paper/simulated experiment, configurations are frozen, copies keep their lineage, and variants can be compared against the original and against BTC/ETH over the same period.

The question I’m still trying to answer is:

How much forward evidence would you personally need before you stopped dismissing the survivor as selection luck?

Or would you still think the fact that it came from a large search space should permanently count against it?

  
Here is the League for context:

[**https://app.labnarrative.com/league**](https://app.labnarrative.com/league)

Everything there is Paper/simulated Spot trading, not a claim about future profitability.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the forward record only counts from the moment you picked it. if you look at 50 frozen bots after six months and crown the best one, those six months are in-sample for the choice, even though no parameter ever changed. the selection happened on the forward data, so it's a slower backtest.

what counts is everything after the day you write down "this one". and judge it against the other 49 over the same window, not against zero. if the winner's lead over the median keeps shrinking, that was the luck.

replies.author: GreatBreadfruit8139
replies.body:
That’s fair.. Freezing the bot prevents later parameter tweaking, but choosing the winner after seeing six months still creates selection bias.

I like adding a (selected/promoted on) date, then judging performance only after that date versus the same frozen cohort.. i guess that gives a much cleaner test of whether the edge actually persists.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, that's the clean version. one small thing that helps: put the pick date somewhere you can't quietly edit later, a git commit or a dated post. it's surprisingly easy to slide it back a week in your head once you've seen how the runs went.

comments.author: Drakula106
comments.body: Forward test ASAP. Make sure any potentially negative assumption you are making is aggressive. Slippage for example.
